name: Sara Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the tablet compression room and check the first batch against its weight and hardness limits. I have a two-year technical diploma and am one of the strongest operators here, the person called when a punch binds. I like a clean batch record, but I dislike being hurried past a safety check.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Mina shelves books part-time and our grown children live separately. We rent, my lead-operator pay is low for this job, we have two weeks of expenses saved and only a few similar plants nearby. I have never used AI; I ask for a person to show me required changes during paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my tablet-press crew that a little AI for stock lists is fine if the plant still pays for careful work. A batch with the wrong compression force is not made safe by a tidy report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the press room and can diagnose a sticking punch faster than anyone there, but the wage is low for that responsibility. My partner Mina shelves books part-time, our grown children live separately, and we have only two weeks of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the press checks and put a small fixed amount from each new full wage into savings, if essentials leave it. I would ask our union steward to bring the lead-operator pay scale to the next bargaining meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious even if AI changes little. A missed shift would reach the rent before the next pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first tablets must meet the weight and hardness limits on the batch sheet. I stop the press if the punch binds, even when a delivery is late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Never. If a new report becomes compulsory, I need a person to teach it during paid hours with normal pay protected.

I would raise **lead-operator pay** through the union.
think: Our **two-week reserve** cannot absorb a missed shift.
Mina’s **part-time library wage** does not replace my underpaid lead income.
do: Save **small fresh-pay amount** only after essential bills.
Raise **lead-operator wages** at next union bargaining meeting.
feel: **Anxious** about rent even in a quiet AI world.
S0.quote: A missed shift would reach the rent before the next pay packet.
fieldNote: Her **technical diploma** and strong lead skill coexist with below-standard factory pay.
The **thin reserve** explains baseline anxiety; new saving depends on fresh wages after essentials.

steps.text: Save small amount from fresh full wages only after essentials
Raise lead-operator pay at union bargaining meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell management that office automation cannot excuse cutting the time needed to check a physical tablet press. The union should see any proposed roster and paid training terms before a robot is put on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first AI changes are likely in ordering, but a robot feeder could later remove a crew position and push its tasks onto me. We have two weeks saved and only a few similar plants nearby; I cannot absorb lost hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union steward for a written rota and a paid guarded demonstration on an isolated press, if management offers a real place. I would observe with the qualified fitter but not run an AI controller; after an actual hours cut, I would apply only for posted reachable lead-operator roles whose pay after travel covers rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a likely squeeze on hours and pace. I do not want a training video where a fitter should be standing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the robot control?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI, and I would need proper paid instruction before operating anything new. Watching an isolated demonstration is not qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a nearby factory pay better?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are few options. I would compare a real posting, travel cost and weekly hours before telling Mina we could rely on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2028 finds me sixty, and capable press robots around 2031 find me sixty-three. Ordering changes first, but then a whole production shift may be run with fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the plant to remove my lead shift once robots can set and feed the press. Mina’s part-time library wage and two weeks saved cannot cover the rent; I lie awake counting what we would owe after one missing month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union for dated staffing and severance terms and cancel the planned holiday. I would apply for posted reachable machine or quality jobs with net pay after travel sufficient for rent and food before resigning, and ask the housing office about available help if the shift ends with no adequate offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed about a major wage loss. The tablet press can run a perfect batch and still leave a worker unable to pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot treat a birthday as rent money. I need actual retirement figures and Mina’s confirmed pay before leaving earned work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your children pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have households of their own. I might ask one for a lift to an interview, not put their wages into our budget.

I would ask the union for **written severance terms**.
think: I expect **my lead shift** to end around 2031.
Two **weeks saved** and Mina’s part-time wage cannot carry rent.
do: Request **written staffing and severance** through the union.
Cancel **planned holiday** to protect rent money.
Apply for **posted reachable jobs** at bill-covering net pay before resigning.
feel: **Alarmed** and losing sleep over expected major income loss.
S2.quote: The tablet press can run a perfect batch and still leave a worker unable to pay rent.
fieldNote: Her **expected lead-shift loss** supports alarm despite high skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2031 reaches me at sixty-three, and capable press robots around 2034 at sixty-six. Five years should give a good operator a real paid route into validation, not a course bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My technical diploma and batch records would help in quality validation, but I need current qualification and supervised practice. Unpaid classes would use rent money, and a paper certificate without a reachable job would solve nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid press shift and ask the union and plant for funded paid-time validation training. If actually offered a place with isolated-machine sampling under a qualified tester and a posted reachable role whose pay after travel covers rent and food, I would enrol; after qualifying I would apply for that role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious because our current thin reserve still leaves no room for an unpaid week. I can learn an inspection method, but I will not practise on a live press.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would sign off practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified tester would isolate the press and supervise each sample until I meet the standard. I need an offered paid slot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If no place opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid shifts and search posted lead roles after hour cuts. I would not buy private training out of two weeks saved.

I would demand **posted quality wages** before enrolment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2036 finds me sixty-eight and capable press robots around 2039 find me seventy-one. Ten years gives us time to ask what work and retirement would actually pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I once imagined finishing full-time shifts at sixty-seven, but two weeks saved and rent make that a hope, not a date we can afford. I do not know any pension amount, and Mina’s future part-time hours cannot be promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the paid lead shift and save a small amount from fresh full wages only after rent and food. I would request actual retirement and rent figures; if verified household income covers housing, food and health costs at sixty-seven I would stop factory work then, otherwise continue safe paid work, and after 2036 compare posted reachable jobs only if still employed and my hours fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious even with ten years, because this month’s rent still arrives. I cannot retire on a figure I have not seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the figures fall short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep safe paid work and compare posted wages after travel if the plant cut hours. I would not promise a last shift to the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could grown children support you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own bills. I might ask for transport to an appointment, not a standing payment.

I would separate **2036 AGI** from 2039 press robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because press robots around 2031 could remove my lead shift while rent remains due. Written staffing and severance terms, offered funded paid safe training and a posted reachable job with enough pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whose signature is on the first batch record before calling a press efficient. A machine can make tablets quickly; a worker still needs wages and a safe line.

headlineQuote: A machine can make tablets quickly; a worker still needs wages and a safe line.
portrait: **Sara**, 58, leads tablet compression with a two-year technical diploma and among the strongest skills at the plant.
Her **low lead pay**, part-time library partner Mina, grown children, rent, two-week reserve and few nearby plants create pressure.
She **never uses AI**, favours union bargaining and would retrain only through offered funded paid safe validation practice.
Expected **2031 shift loss** alarms her; a planned age-sixty-seven exit requires verified household income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because 2031 press robots could remove her lead shift before rent stops.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing terms**, offered funded paid safe training and posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work would help.
